unit.title: Coordinate and manage basic installation projects

summary: This unit teaches you to coordinate and manage a basic installation project, such as putting up a steel canopy, shed frame, mezzanine or handrails on site. You will learn to set the project up, plan the programme and resources, lay out the site and work with the client and other trades, control safety, hot work and lifting, manage materials and quality with hold points, track progress, cost, changes and delays, and hand the finished work over with its records and a review of lessons learned.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). An **installation project** takes fabricated steelwork out of the shop and fixes it in place on site: a canopy over a school entrance, a shed frame, a warehouse mezzanine, a set of handrails at a supermarket. The steel may be perfect, and the job can still fail: bolts cast in the wrong place, a crane booked for a day the bases are not ready, a fire started beside a timber store, or a client who was never told the entrance would be closed.

The **project coordinator** makes the parts fit together: the drawings, the people, the plant, the materials, the other trades, the client and the public, safely, on time and within the budget. At Level 3 you may coordinate a small project yourself, or run part of a larger one for a supervisor.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 welders, fabricators and team leaders who plan and run site installation work.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Check the scope, approved drawings, approvals and contract; visit the site; hold a start-up meeting.
List the tasks, work out durations and crew sizes, find the critical path and float, set milestones and hold points, book people and plant.
Set up the site and coordinate others
Lay out cranes, deliveries and storage; agree the order of work with the builder and other trades; keep the client and neighbours informed.
Risk assessment and method statement, hot-work permits and fire watch, safe work at height, barriers for the public, emergency arrangements.
A lift plan with masses and safe working loads, a certified crane and operator, one signaller, an exclusion zone and weather checks.
Staged deliveries, piece marks and storage; inspection and test plan with hold points; qualified welders; non-conformances dealt with properly.
Keep a site diary, compare work done and money spent with the plan, deal with delays and variations, report honestly.
Clear the site, list and fix snags with the client, hand over the records, and review the lessons learned.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on setting up, roles, coordinating trades, approvals, the programme, resources, people, site safety, hot work, lifting, risk, records, changes, progress and cost, delays, subcontractors, quality, handover and review, with some calculations.

A **written paper** with short answers (method statement, lift plan, holding-down bolts, fire watch, float, hold point, MEWP, SWL, lessons learned, hot-work permit, and calculations of cost, mass, quantities, percentages and dates) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Two group practicals:** plan a steel canopy installation (Gantt chart, risk assessment and method statement, outline lift plan, delivery plan and bolt list, inspection plan) and run a start-up meeting; and coordinate a staged installation of a small frame at the Centre, with hold-point checks, a site diary and a handover.

blocks.note: Many questions ask what the coordinator should do **first**. Usually the answer is to make things safe, get the facts, and tell the people affected, before anyone starts fixing the problem in their own way.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The project and the coordinator's role

flow: Start-up: scope, drawings, approvals, contract and site visit agreed
Plan: programme, resources, safety documents, lift plan, materials and quality plans
Do and monitor: deliver, erect, inspect, record, and correct as you go
Close: snags fixed, handover with records, site cleared, lessons learned

head: Role
Their part in the project
rows: Owns and pays for the work; gives access; approves changes to the scope; accepts the work at handover
Designs the structure; approves drawings and any change to them; inspects or signs off key connections
Runs the wider site; casts the bases and holding-down bolts; coordinates all trades
Plans and organises the installation; books people and plant; coordinates trades and the client; controls safety, quality, cost and records
Carry out the work to the drawings, the WPS and the method statement
Crane hire, galvanising, painting, scaffolding and other specialist work
Checks the work at the hold points and signs it off
The municipal corporation gives building approval and may inspect

blocks.p: The coordinator's job is to organise, not to do everyone else's work. Booking the crane, agreeing the lift date, chasing the galvaniser and keeping the records are coordination tasks; running the root pass on a splice belongs to a qualified welder.

ul: The **scope** says exactly what is included and what is not, for example: "supply and erect the canopy frame and roof sheeting; bases and holding-down bolts by the builder; lights by the electrician". Anything outside it is a change.

A structure such as a shed, canopy or mezzanine usually needs **building approval** from the municipal corporation. The client normally obtains it, but the coordinator checks it is in place before work starts: work without approval may have to be stopped or even taken down.
Check that the drawings are **approved for construction** by the engineer, not preliminary drawings.
Keep a drawing register showing the current revision of each drawing.
When a new revision arrives, remove the old copies from the site or mark them SUPERSEDED, and tell the crew what has changed.
Only the current revision is used for setting out, fabrication and checking.
Keep the project documents together: scope and contract, drawings, specifications, WPS, programme, risk assessment and method statement, lift plan, permits, inspection records and the site diary.

blocks.p: List every task, from setting out and checking the bases to handover. Work out each duration from the **labour hours** it needs:

ul: **Duration (days) = labour hours ÷ (number of people × hours per day).** Erecting a frame needs 120 labour hours; with a crew of 5 working 8-hour days: 120 ÷ (5 × 8) = 3 days.
**Crew size = labour hours ÷ (days × hours per day).** To finish the same 120 hours in 2 days: 120 ÷ (2 × 8) = 7.5, so 8 people, if there is room and equipment for them to work safely.
Adding people does not always shorten a task: one crane, one splice or one narrow access can only take so many.

blocks.h: Order of work, the critical path and float

blocks.p: Some tasks cannot start until others finish; others can run side by side. Draw them on a **Gantt chart**: a bar for each task against the calendar.

head: Task
Duration
Can start after
Start–finish (day)
rows: C Bolt up, plumb and line
E Fabricate gates in the shop

ul: The **critical path** is the longest chain of linked tasks: A → B → C → D = 4 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 12 days. Any delay on it delays the finish.

**Float** is how long a task can slip without delaying the finish. F must be done by day 12 and takes 1 day, so it may start as late as day 11: it has 2 days of float. E finishes on day 4 but is not needed until day 9: it has 5 days of float.
Watch the critical tasks most closely, and use float to move work that is not critical when people or plant clash.
A **milestone** is a key point in the programme with no duration of its own, used to check progress: bases passed, steel delivered, columns erected and plumbed, roof on, handover.
Put inspections in the programme as tasks. A **hold point** is a stage past which work must not go until the inspection is done and signed; work above cannot start until it is passed.

blocks.p: Count working days on a calendar, leaving out weekends (if the crew does not work them) and public holidays. Jamaica's public holidays are New Year's Day, Ash Wednesday, Good Friday, Easter Monday, Labour Day (23 May), Emancipation Day (1 August), Independence Day (6 August), National Heroes Day (third Monday in October), Christmas Day and Boxing Day. Check the published list each year, as some dates move.

head: Resource
Points to plan
rows: Enough crew; welders qualified for each joint and position on the drawings; riggers and a trained signaller; a first aider
Engine-driven welders, generator, crane, MEWP or scaffold, cutting sets, torque wrench (in calibration); book early; avoid clashes between jobs
Steel in erection order, bolts with spares, consumables, paint for touch-up
The budget, with a **contingency**: an amount kept back for things that cannot be foreseen, such as 8% of a J$1 250 000 budget = J$100 000

blocks.note: When one piece of plant is needed by two jobs at the same time, re-plan one job's work, use float, or hire a second unit. Never let two teams "share" by moving a machine at lunchtime: both jobs end up behind.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Setting up the site and working with others

blocks.p: Visit the site with the client before planning in detail. Look at access for trucks and the crane, the ground, overhead lines, the client's own activities, neighbours, water and power, storage space and security.

ul: **Crane position**, with firm ground for its outriggers, and its lifting radius.
**Delivery route** and unloading point, kept clear, avoiding busy times such as school drop-off.
**Laydown area** for steel, on bearers, near the crane, out of walkways.
**Welfare:** toilets, drinking water, shade and a place to eat.
**Site hut and locked store** for bolts, tools, consumables; a ventilated, locked cylinder store.
**Engine-driven welder or generator** outdoors, with the exhaust pointing away from people, doors and windows, and away from the fuel store.
**Exclusion zones**, barriers, signs, the emergency route and the assembly point.
**Waste bins**, kept apart by type.

head: Trade
What to agree
rows: A bolt setting plan or template for the holding-down bolts; check position, level and projection before the concrete is poured and again before erection; time for the concrete to cure
Positions of their brackets and cleats at the planning stage, so they are welded in the shop instead of drilled or welded on site after painting
When the frame will be inspected and passed, so they can follow on
Touch-up after all site welding is finished
One programme for all trades; a short weekly coordination meeting; changes sent in writing; hot work planned so that nobody is working below or beside it

blocks.p: Before work starts, hold a meeting with the crew and the client to go through the scope, programme, roles, contacts, site rules, working hours, access, safety arrangements and the dates of any closures. Take minutes with actions, owners and dates.

blocks.h: The client, the public and the neighbours

ul: Agree working hours and areas with the client, especially where a school, shop or clinic stays open.
Give notice **well in advance**, with the date, time and route, of anything that affects the client: an entrance closed for a lift, a power cut, a noisy day.
Plan noisy and spark-producing work for quiet periods agreed with the client.
Screen sparks and arc light from the public; control noise and dust; no burning of waste.
Keep the site tidy and secure at the end of every day.

blocks.note: Many installation jobs in Jamaica are done at schools, churches, clinics, shops and hotels that stay open while the work goes on. Plan lifts and hot work around class times, services, opening hours and guests, and agree them with the client in writing.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: A **risk assessment** lists the hazards of the job, who could be harmed and how, and the controls that bring each risk down.
A **method statement** sets out each step of the work in order, with its hazards, controls, equipment and who does what. Together they are often called RAMS.
Every hazard named must have a control, and the crew is briefed on both before work starts. A short toolbox talk each morning covers the day's tasks.

flow: Hot-work permit issued for the area and the day
Area checked: anything that burns removed or covered with fire blankets, as far as the permit says (often about 10 m); gaps and cracks checked
Screens up; barriers and signs keep people away
A trained fire watch with a suitable extinguisher during the work
The fire watch stays on after work stops, for the time the permit gives (often 30 to 60 minutes), checking for smouldering
Area checked again and the permit closed and signed

ul: Welding needs both hands and a steady stance: use a tagged scaffold or tower, or a MEWP with a trained operator. Never ladders, pallets or racking.
Check the scaffold tag before the crew uses it every day.
Where work is overhead of people, close the area below, or provide a covered walkway and barriers.
Engine-driven welders and generators give off carbon monoxide: keep them outdoors, exhaust away from openings.
Refuel only with the engine stopped and cooled, with no hot work or smoking nearby, and wipe up spills.
Store fuel apart from gas cylinders and hot work.
Gas cylinders stay upright and chained, with oxygen apart from fuel gas, and go into a ventilated, locked store overnight.

flow: Make the area safe, without putting yourself in danger
Call for help: 110 for fire and ambulance, 119 for police; send someone to meet the ambulance
A trained first aider gives first aid; do not move a person who may have a back or neck injury unless they are in danger
Keep others away and stop work in the area
Report to the manager and the client; record it; keep the scene as it was if the injury is serious
Investigate the cause and put controls in place

blocks.p: **Near misses** are recorded and investigated in the same way: a bolt falling near a car or a person is a warning of the accident that could happen next.

blocks.note: Site crews in Jamaica work in heat and strong sun. Plan water, shade and rest breaks, and start heavy work early in the day where the client allows. Heat stress makes people careless and slow to spot danger.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Every crane lift needs a written **lift plan**, prepared by a competent person and agreed before the day. It states:

ul: The **mass** of each load, including the lifting gear (slings, shackles, spreader beam) hanging from the hook.
The crane's **capacity at the radius** needed, from the crane's load chart.
The slings and shackles, each with a **safe working load (SWL)** above the load it will carry, and the lifting points on the steel.
The crane position, the ground under its outriggers, and the mats or timbers needed.
Overhead lines and other hazards, and the clearances to keep.
The exclusion zone, the one trained **signaller**, tag lines, and the sequence of lifts.
The wind limit for the crane and the load, and who decides to stop.
Section mass = mass per metre × length: a rafter 8.4 m long at 38 kg/m weighs 8.4 × 38 = 319.2 kg.
Add the lifting gear: with 15 kg of slings and shackles, the hook load is about 334 kg.
Plate parts: area × thickness × 7850 kg/m³.
Ask for the crane's current examination and test certificates, the operator's proof of competence, and insurance.
Check the hire terms. Cranes often have a minimum charge: at J$21 000 an hour with a 3-hour minimum and J$12 000 travel, a 2-hour lift costs 3 × 21 000 + 12 000 = J$75 000.
Confirm the crane only when the bases have passed inspection and the steel is on site; a crane standing idle is paid for by the hour.

flow: Brief the whole crew on the lift plan and each person's role
Check the weather against the crane's wind limit; be ready to postpone
Check the crane is set up on firm ground with its outriggers on mats, and the exclusion zone is barricaded
Check the slings, shackles and lifting points
Trial lift: raise the load just clear of the ground and stop, to check the balance, the slings and the crane
Lift smoothly on the signaller's signals only; steady the load with tag lines from outside the zone
Land the load and fix it (bolts in and snug) before the slings are released

blocks.note: Nobody stands or walks under a suspended load, for any reason. If a load must be guided into place, it is steadied with tag lines from a safe position, and hands go on it only when it is just above its final position.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Deliver in stages, in **erection order**, so the site is not blocked and the first parts needed come off the truck first.
Every part carries its **piece mark** from the drawings, and every load comes with a packing list. Unmarked parts get fitted in the wrong place.
Check each delivery against the packing list and the drawings, and record damage at once.
Store steel off the ground on timber bearers, where water drains away; protect painted and galvanised parts from sling damage with soft slings and packing; cover them if they must wait.
Near the sea, salt air quickly attacks bare or damaged steel: plan short storage times and touch up damage promptly.
Lock bolts, small fittings, consumables and tools away.

blocks.p: An **inspection and test plan (ITP)** lists every check: what is checked, when, by whom, against what, and which record is kept. A **hold point** stops the work until the check is passed and signed. A **witness point** means the inspector is told in advance and may attend; the ITP says whether work may go on if they do not come.

head: Stage
Check
Why it matters
rows: Bases and holding-down bolts: position, level and projection against the drawing
A base fault throws out the whole frame
Piece marks, sizes, coating and damage against the delivery note and drawings
The right part goes in the right place
Plumb and line, within the tolerance on the drawing or specification, before the beams go on
Easy to adjust now, hard later
Bolt grade, washers and tightening; torque checked with a calibrated torque wrench where the drawing gives a value, and recorded
Loose or under-strength bolts make a weak connection
Visual inspection by the welder and the inspector; dye penetrant (PT) or magnetic particle (MT) testing for surface cracks where the drawing asks
Defects found before they are covered
The whole frame passed and signed
Faults are easy to fix before they are hidden

ul: Only welders **qualified** for the joint, process and position may weld it; a welder without the right qualification is given other work.
A torque wrench must be within its calibration date. If it is out of date, its readings cannot be trusted: replace it and re-check the bolts it was used on.

flow: Stop the affected work; do not force, cut or bodge it
Measure, photograph and record the problem
Report it in writing to the main contractor and the client, and ask the engineer for the solution
Re-plan the crew onto other work meanwhile
Carry out the engineer's written instruction, then have it inspected
Record the extra time and cost; if the fault was not yours, it is a variation

ul: A **variation** is any change to the scope, the design or the method: an extra landing, a lighter beam, a different finish.
Design changes are approved by the design engineer in writing; changes to the scope by the client in writing.
Agree the effect on price and time before the work is done, and record it.
A spoken request on site, however friendly, is written down and confirmed before the crew acts on it.

blocks.p: Keep a **site diary** every day: the weather; the crew and hours; plant on site; work done; deliveries; visitors and inspections; instructions received; delays and their causes; incidents and near misses; and dated photos. It is the record that settles arguments later, such as when damage happened or why a day was lost.

ul: Set a **baseline** at the start: the programme, the planned labour hours for each stage, and the budget.
Measure work done in real units: columns erected, connections welded, square metres sheeted. 14 of 20 connections welded = 14 ÷ 20 × 100 = 70% complete.
Compare the share of the work done with the share of the hours or money used. If 40% of the work is done but 55% of the hours are used, the job is behind and over its labour budget.
**Overspend (%) = (actual − budget) ÷ budget × 100.** Budget J$640 000, actual J$704 000: 64 000 ÷ 640 000 × 100 = 10% over.

flow: Find out early, from the site diary and the weekly comparison
Find the cause: late steel, rain, a missing crane, rework, bases not ready
Tell the client and the manager at once, with the facts
Re-plan: move the crew to work that can go ahead, use float, add people or hours if the budget allows
Chase the supplier or subcontractor; agree a new date if needed
Record the delay and, if it was not your fault, claim the time and cost as a variation

blocks.p: Report to the manager and the client every week, in the same short format: progress against the programme, cost against the budget, problems and the actions being taken, risks ahead, and decisions needed. Report honestly: bad news given early can still be managed.

ul: Agree their scope, dates and price in writing.
Before they start, get their risk assessment and method statement, and proof of competence, certificates and insurance.
Give them the site induction and the site rules.
Supervise and check their work as you would your own; it is part of your project.
Finish every task, including touch-up painting after the last site weld.
Clear the site: offcuts, rod stubs, packing and waste, disposed of the right way; paint tins and solvent rags as hazardous waste.
Carry out a final inspection against the drawings and the ITP.

flow: Walk round the finished work with the client
List any snags (small defects or unfinished items) together, each with a date to fix it
Fix the snags and check them off with the client
Explain how to care for the structure and its limits
Hand over the records and get the handover form signed

head: Handover record
Why it matters
rows: Show exactly what was built, including any changes, so anyone altering or repairing it later knows what is there
Inspection and test records (welds, bolt torques, NDT)
Prove the work met the standard
Material certificates, where the job needs them
So touch-ups and repainting use a compatible system
The client knows who to call and what is covered
Design load limits; regular paint checks; no cutting, drilling, welding or extra loads (such as tanks or signs) without the engineer's approval

blocks.p: After handover there is usually a **defects period** in the contract (often several months to a year) in which the installer must put right any defects that appear. Keep copies of every record in the job file.

ul: Gather the facts: programme against actual dates, budget against actual cost, the site diary, variations and incident reports.
Hold a short close-out meeting with the crew, and the client if possible. Look at what went well and what went wrong, and find causes without blaming people.
Agree specific actions, such as booking galvanising earlier with a buffer, or checking bolts before the pour.
Write them up as **lessons learned**, share them, and build them into the planning checklist and the price for the next job.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can describe the stages of an installation project and the roles of the client, engineer, builder, coordinator, crew, subcontractors and inspector.
I can check the scope, approved drawings and building approval before work starts, and control drawing revisions.
I can work out durations and crew sizes from labour hours.
I can draw a simple Gantt chart, find the critical path and work out float.
I can set milestones and put hold points in the programme, and count working days around Jamaica's public holidays.
I can plan people, plant, materials and a contingency, and deal with clashes.
I can plan a site layout and coordinate the builder and other trades, including the holding-down bolts.
I can keep the client, the public and the neighbours informed and protected.
I can prepare a risk assessment and method statement, and control hot work with a permit and fire watch.
I can plan safe work at height and the safe use of plant, fuel and gas on site.
I can respond to an incident and report near misses.
I can plan and control a crane lift, including the hook load, the crane papers, a trial lift and the exclusion zone.
I can plan staged deliveries and protect steel on site.
I can use an inspection and test plan with hold points, and deal with a non-conformance.
I can handle variations correctly, in writing.
I can keep a site diary, measure progress and cost against the plan, and deal with delays.
I can hand over the work with a snag list and the right records, and lead a lessons-learned review.

terms: As-built drawings
Drawings that show the work exactly as it was finally built
Baseline
The original programme and budget against which progress is measured
Contingency
An amount kept back in the budget for things that cannot be foreseen
Critical path
The longest chain of linked tasks; a delay on it delays the finish
Exclusion zone
A barricaded area people must not enter during lifting or other dangerous work
Fire watch
A person who watches for fire during hot work and for a set time after it
Float
How long a task can slip without delaying the finish date
Gantt chart
A bar chart showing each task against the calendar
Holding-down bolts
Bolts cast into a concrete base to fix a column's base plate
Hold point
A stage that work must not pass until an inspection has been done and signed
Hot-work permit
A written permit, issued before welding or cutting, confirming the fire precautions
ITP
Inspection and test plan: the list of checks, who does them, when, and the records
Lessons learned
What a team would do differently next time, recorded after a project
Lift plan
The written plan for a crane lift: load, crane, gear, area, people and limits
Method statement
A step-by-step description of how the work will be done safely
MEWP
Mobile elevating work platform, such as a scissor lift or boom lift
Milestone
A key point in the programme used to check progress
Near miss
An event that could have hurt someone but did not
Non-conformance
Work or material that does not meet the drawing or specification
Piece mark
The mark on each fabricated part showing where it goes
Scope
What the project includes and what it does not
Site diary
A daily record of work, people, weather, deliveries, events and instructions
Snag list
A list of small defects or unfinished items to put right before handover
SWL
Safe working load: the most a piece of lifting gear may carry
Variation
A change to the scope, design or method of the work

c1.title: A school canopy in Oracabessa
c1.text: Fitzroy Watson is coordinating a steel canopy over the walkway of a primary school in Oracabessa, St Mary. His programme has six tasks: A, the builder casts and cures the bases (5 days); B, erect the columns (3 days, after A); C, fix the beams and purlins (2 days, after B); D, roof sheeting (4 days, after C); E, fabricate the handrails in the shop (6 days, starting on day 1); F, fit the handrails (1 day, after both C and E). The canopy beams must be lifted in by a mobile crane over the school's main walkway, and the school is in term.

c2.title: A warehouse mezzanine in Lionel Town
c2.text: Ms Nordia Walters is coordinating a steel mezzanine in a warehouse in Lionel Town, Clarendon. The drawing gives a tightening torque for the column base bolts; the crew's torque wrench has a calibration sticker that ran out last year. The inspector's visual check of the site welds finds undercut deeper than the code allows on 2 of the 14 beam connections, and the flooring contractor wants to start laying the deck tomorrow. During a site visit the warehouse owner asks the welders to add a small extra landing at the top of the stairs, "while you're here".

c3.title: Handrails at a supermarket in Papine
c3.text: Romaine Clarke is coordinating the installation of new steel handrails and a ramp at a supermarket in Papine, St Andrew, which stays open from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. The welding will be done near the store's stack of baled cardboard, using a hired engine-driven welder, which will need refuelling halfway through each day. The store manager has complained about the noise of grinding during the morning rush. On the second day, a shopper ducks under the barrier to take a short cut past the welders.

c4.title: Lifting a beam in Porus
c4.text: Kirk Brown is planning the lift of a 9 m steel beam onto two columns for a farm shed in Porus, Manchester. The supplier's table gives the beam's mass as 52 kg per metre, and the slings and shackles weigh 18 kg in all. The hired mobile crane will stand at the edge of the yard, where one of its outriggers would land on ground that was filled and levelled only last month. The crew includes two welders who will bolt the beam to the columns once it is in place.

c5.title: Handing over a clinic shade in Claremont
c5.text: Mr Barrington Lewis is coordinating a steel shade structure over the outdoor waiting area of a health clinic in Claremont, St Ann. The clinic's administrator, Mrs Simone Reid, often asks why the work is not further on. As the work nears its end, Mr Lewis prepares the handover pack, and Mrs Reid asks whether the clinic can later hang a large plastic water tank from the new frame.

questions.q: How long is the critical path of Fitzroy's programme?
o: 21 days
14 days
15 days
11 days
questions.why: A → B → C → D is 5 + 3 + 2 + 4 = 14 days, the longest chain of linked tasks. Adding every task together (21 days) ignores the tasks that run side by side.

questions.q: How much float does task E (fabricating the handrails) have?
o: 0 days
6 days
3 days
4 days
questions.why: C finishes on day 10, so F can start then. E takes 6 days from the start, finishing on day 6, so it can slip 10 − 6 = 4 days before it holds up F. F itself has 3 days of float before the day-14 finish.

questions.q: The builder says the bases will be 3 days late. What does this mean for the canopy?
o: The finish slips 3 days, as A is on the critical path
Nothing, as the handrail work has float to absorb it
Only the handrails will be late, by 3 days
The finish slips 6 days, as every task after A doubles
questions.why: Task A is on the critical path, so every day it slips moves the finish by a day. Fitzroy tells the school at once, re-books the crane for the new date, and looks for ways to win time back later in the programme.

questions.q: When should Fitzroy plan the crane lift over the school's main walkway?
o: When pupils are away, agreed with the school ahead
During morning assembly, when the walkway is quiet
Whenever the crane is free, with a teacher on watch
During a lesson, with the walkway taped off for an hour
questions.why: No load may pass over people, and children are hard to keep out of an area. Lifting at a weekend, a holiday or another time when pupils are away, agreed in writing well in advance, removes the risk.

questions.q: What should Ms Walters do about the out-of-date torque wrench?
o: Use it, as torque wrenches do not drift over time
Tighten each nut a little beyond the drawing value
Use a calibrated wrench and re-check the bolts
Have the strongest fitter tighten the nuts by feel
questions.why: A wrench out of calibration may read wrongly, so its results cannot be trusted or recorded. A calibrated wrench is used, the bolts it tightened are re-checked, and the readings are written in the inspection record.

questions.q: The flooring contractor wants to start tomorrow. What should happen?
o: Let the flooring start, as only 2 of the 14 connections are affected
Hold it until the welds are repaired and signed off
Let the flooring start and repair the welds from below later
Ask the flooring contractor to inspect the welds as they go
questions.why: The inspection of the frame is a hold point: work that would cover or load it waits until it passes. Repairing undercut is easy now and hard once the deck is on, and the signed record proves the frame is right.

questions.q: How should Ms Walters deal with the owner's request for an extra landing?
o: Treat it as a variation, agreed in writing first
Let the welders add it now, to keep the owner happy
Refuse, as nothing can be added once a job has started
Add it, then send the owner a bill at the end of the job
questions.why: An extra landing changes the scope and the design. It needs the engineer's design and the client's written instruction, with the price and time agreed, before the crew starts. A spoken request on site is not enough.

questions.q: Before the welding starts near the baled cardboard, what must be in place?
o: A permit, cardboard cleared, screens, a fire watch
A bucket of water beside the welder and a sign on the bales
Only the welder's own PPE, as the bales are a few metres away
A promise from the store to move the bales if they catch fire
questions.why: Baled cardboard burns fiercely and sparks travel far. The hot-work permit checks that combustibles are moved or covered, screens are up, an extinguisher is at hand and a fire watch stays during and after the work.

questions.q: How should the engine-driven welder be refuelled?
o: With the engine running, so the welding is not interrupted
Quickly, while the welder takes a short break from the arc
Beside the welding area, so the fuel can is close to hand
Engine off and cool, with no hot work nearby
questions.why: Fuel spilled on a hot engine or reached by a spark can catch fire. The engine is stopped and allowed to cool, there is no hot work or smoking nearby, and any spill is wiped up before restarting.

questions.q: How should Romaine respond to the manager's complaint about grinding noise?
o: Carry on, as grinding is a normal part of the work
Stop all grinding and leave the welds unground
Agree quiet times with him and grind then
Do the grinding late at night without telling the manager
questions.why: Where a business stays open, the coordinator agrees with the client when noisy and spark-producing work is done, such as before opening, and plans the programme around it. Quality must not suffer, so the grinding still gets done.

questions.q: What should happen when the shopper ducks under the barrier?
o: Carry on welding, as the shopper chose to come in
Stop work, see the shopper out, fix the barrier
Shout at the shopper and carry on with the weld
Take the barrier down, as people will ignore it anyway
questions.why: Sparks, arc light and moving steel can hurt anyone inside the zone. Work stops until the person is safely out; then the barrier is made harder to cross or a marshal is posted, and the near miss is recorded.

questions.q: What load should Kirk's lift plan allow for at the crane hook?
o: About 468 kg
About 61 kg
About 4 680 kg
About 486 kg
questions.why: The beam is 9 m × 52 kg/m = 468 kg, and the slings and shackles hanging from the hook add 18 kg: about 486 kg. The crane's capacity at the radius needed must be above this.

questions.q: What should be done about the outrigger position on the newly filled ground?
o: Nothing, as the crane's outriggers spread the load well
Lift quickly, so the ground has no time to settle
Have the ground checked, and use mats or move the crane
Put the outrigger on a few loose blocks to raise it
questions.why: Fresh fill can sink under an outrigger and tip the crane. The ground's strength is checked, and the lift plan uses outrigger mats or timbers to spread the load, or moves the crane to firm ground.

questions.q: Before the beam is swung over to the columns, what should the crew do?
o: Lift it straight to full height to save the crane's time
Lift it just clear of the ground and stop, to check it
Have a welder ride on the beam to steady it in the air
Swing it quickly so it does not have time to spin
questions.why: A trial lift, just clear of the ground, shows whether the beam hangs level, the slings are seated and the crane's brakes hold, while it is still safe to lower it and adjust.

questions.q: As the beam comes down onto the columns, how should the welders guide it?
o: By standing under it and pushing it into line
By climbing onto the columns early and catching it
With tag lines, from outside the zone
By pulling it over with the welding leads
questions.why: Nobody stands under a suspended load. Tag lines steady and turn the beam from a safe position; hands go on it only when it is just above its seats, and it is bolted before the slings are released.

questions.q: Mrs Reid asks why the work is not further on. Which record lets Mr Lewis answer with facts?
o: The crew's training certificates and qualifications
The steel supplier's price list for the year
The original tender drawings from before approval
The site diary, with its dated daily entries
questions.why: The site diary records each day's work, crew, weather, deliveries, instructions and delays. With it, Mr Lewis can show what happened and why, and compare progress with the programme honestly.

questions.q: Why should the as-built drawings go into the handover pack?
o: They record what was really built on site
They prove the welders were paid the right amount
They are needed to order the next steel job
They show the colour the steel will be repainted
questions.why: Changes made on site mean the original drawings may no longer match the structure. As-built drawings record what is actually there, so later repairs and alterations start from the truth.

questions.q: How should Mr Lewis answer Mrs Reid's question about the water tank?
o: Yes, as steel frames can carry almost any load
Only after the engineer checks the frame
Yes, if the tank is hung from the middle of a beam
No, as nothing may ever be fixed to a steel frame
questions.why: The frame was designed for set loads, and a full tank weighs a great deal. The care instructions in the handover pack say that extra loads, cutting, drilling and welding need the engineer's assessment first.

questions.q: A painting crew is booked to start on Monday 8 February 2027 for 5 working days, Monday to Friday. Ash Wednesday, 10 February 2027, is a public holiday. On what day should the painting finish?
o: Friday 12 February
Thursday 11 February
Tuesday 16 February
Monday 15 February
questions.why: The working days are Monday 8, Tuesday 9, Thursday 11, Friday 12 and Monday 15 February, skipping the Ash Wednesday holiday and the weekend. Forgetting the holiday gives Friday 12 February.

questions.q: A painting subcontractor arrives on site without a risk assessment or method statement. What should the coordinator do?
o: Let them start and ask for the papers by the end of the week
Let them start, as painting is low-risk work
Hold the start until both are given, checked and briefed
Write the papers for them and let them begin at once
questions.why: A subcontractor's work is part of the project, and its hazards (solvents, work at height, fire) must be assessed and controlled. Work starts only when the papers are received, checked and explained to the crew.
